title.narrative: NIHR Development Awards Call 1: Improving Outcomes for Patients with Fragility Fractures in the Philippines

description.narrative:
A low- and-middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the University of the Philippines Manila, Philippines in partnership with the University of Oxford, United Kingdom which aims to convene a community engagement group to explore and understand patient, carer, and healthcare provider experiences and priorities, map existing care pathways, and develop strategies to enhance recovery from fragility fractures.
Commencing in January 2025, this twelve-month award will undertake patient and carer interviews and hospital surveys to identify the facilities currently available for treating these patients in the Philippines. This work will inform a subsequent research proposal to improve patient outcomes, reduce healthcare costs, and influence national healthcare policy in the Philippines and other LMICs in Southeast Asia.
The number of people with fragility fractures is increasing in many LMICs. Asia is particularly affected by rapidly aging populations; a study in nine countries predicts a two-fold increase in the number of hip fractures alone, from just over a million in 2018 to more than two and a half million by 2050. Data from the Orthogeriatric and Fracture Liaison Service registry of the Philippine General Hospital show significant healthcare costs, with an estimated economic burden of PhP 1 billion per year (approximately USD 17 million). This may underrate the real situation, as the majority of hip fractures are still underreported due to economic and logistical reasons, and osteoporosis and fragility fracture treatment is not a priority of the Philippine healthcare system at present. No cost-effective treatment pathway of care for patients with fragility fractures is in place in the Philippines. Unlike hip fractures, most patients with a shoulder, wrist, or ankle fracture are not admitted to hospital but are treated as outpatients via the hospital fracture clinic; these patients’ disabilities compromise independence, quality of life, and productivity as well.

This award has three objectives:
1. To expand the existing Philippines Community Engagement and Involvement Group to include patients with shoulder, wrist, and ankle fractures and conduct in-depth interviews with patients aged 50 and above, and carers or family members. By exploring their experiences, challenges, and priorities during their recovery this will help identify key points in the care pathway where targeted interventions can improve outcomes. 2. To map capabilities in managing fragility fractures, particularly those involving the shoulder, wrist, and ankle through a comprehensive survey assessing service availability and service-specific readiness using the World Health Organisation Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) tool. 3. To create bespoke country-specific data to influence and change policy at a national and regional level to improve care for all patients with fragility fractures.
